title: Q15 Calculator
description: Q15 stores a number from -1.0 up to just under +1.0 as a 16-bit integer q that stands for q / 32,768, so 16,384 is 0.5. Multiplying two Q15 numbers gives a 30-bit product that must be shifted right by 15 bits to return to Q15: result = (a x b) >> 15. The shift keeps the sign and rounds toward minus infinity, and one product (-1.0 x -1.0) does not fit back into 16 bits.

learningObjectives: The learner will calculate the Q15 product (a x b) >> 15 of 6 pairs of Q15 integers, and state whether the result fits in 16 bits, with at least 5 of 6 correct.
prerequisites: fixed-point math, Q15 format, arithmetic shift right (all defined in this chapter above the block).

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Explore, then fixed-order practice items with one attempt each and immediate explained feedback
keyQuestions: Is the product of two Q15 numbers already a Q15 number?
Why is (-3 x 3) >> 15 equal to -1 and not 0?
Why can Q15 hold -1.0 but not +1.0?
commonMisconceptions: (1) The product of two Q15 numbers is already Q15. (2) A shift right always rounds toward zero. (3) Q15 can hold exactly 1.0.
assessmentOpportunities: Complete all six pairs. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.
